RE: CMS-0062-P; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Dear Administrator: 
McKesson Corporation (“McKesson”) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for 
Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule on Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs. We commend CMS for continuing to advance policies that modernize 
healthcare data exchange, reduce administrative burden, and improve timely access to care. 
McKesson is a diversified healthcare services organization with a unique enterprise-wide perspective 
spanning community pharmacy, specialty care, oncology, distribution, and health information 
technology. We partner across the healthcare ecosystem—including providers, pharmacies, payers, 
and technology developers—to improve patient access, affordability, and outcomes. 
We strongly support CMS’s effort to extend interoperability and electronic prior authorization (ePA) 
requirements to prescription drugs. As reflected in our prior comments on health technology policy, prior 
authorization for drugs remains a significant driver of administrative burden, care delays, and 
fragmentation across the healthcare system. Expanding standardized, electronic, and API-enabled 
workflows to drugs is a critical step toward improving efficiency and advancing patient-centered care. At 
the same time, successful implementation will depend on ensuring that the rule reflects real-world 
workflows across the full healthcare ecosystem—including pharmacies, PBMs, providers, and 
interoperability vendors—rather than narrowly focusing on EHR-based environments.  
 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
McKesson recognizes CMS’s efforts to modernize prior authorization for drugs and reduce 
administrative burden through expanded electronic workflows. The proposed rule represents an 
important opportunity to improve interoperability, streamline processes, and support more timely patient 
access to care. 
To maximize its impact, CMS should prioritize full transition of pharmacy benefit prior authorizations to 
electronic workflows, eliminating reliance on fax and requiring consistent use of existing ePA

infrastructure. CMS should also require payers and PBMs to provide machine-readable coverage 
criteria at the point of initial eligibility inquiry and ensure alignment between payer medical policies and 
PBM prior authorization requirements. CMS should require PBM and Payer APIs to provide patient-
specific responses that are machine-readable. Ideally, the provider interaction point would use patient 
identifiers to surface the anticipated or understood benefit eligibility and coverage information. The 
payer then could respond back with confirmation, clarifications, or corrections to the patient-specific 
coverage to streamline the process of coverage determination. 
In addition, the rule should preserve a dual-standard framework that leverages both FHIR and NCPDP 
standards, enable participation from pharmacies and broader care teams in electronic workflows, and 
require more actionable and transparent payer responses. Finally, CMS should adopt phased 
implementation timelines with clear, defined expectations that reflect operational readiness while 
maintaining momentum toward full electronic adoption. 
 
I. BACKGROUND AND OVERVIEW 
McKesson supports CMS’s overall direction and agrees that prior authorization for drugs is a major 
contributor to administrative burden and delays in patient care. Addressing these workflows through 
standardized, interoperable approaches is essential to improving access and system efficiency. 
 
II. PROVISIONS OF THE PROPOSED RULE AND MCKESSON COMMENTS 
Section II.A. Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) 
Section II.A.2. National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) Standards for Prior 
Authorization of Drugs Covered Under a Pharmacy Benefit 
McKesson supports CMS’s efforts to standardize APIs and promote consistent implementation across 
payers. We applaud CMS for recognizing that APIs must serve as core infrastructure for interoperable 
prior authorization workflows, enabling real-time access to prior authorization status, visibility into 
benefit design and utilization controls, and seamless data exchange across providers, pharmacies, and 
third-party tools. 
 
To achieve these objectives, CMS should ensure that implementation requirements include adequate 
transition timelines, clear and machine-readable documentation, and performance metrics that reflect 
actual workflow integration rather than technical availability alone. These guardrails are essential to 
avoiding fragmentation and ensuring that APIs function effectively in real-world environments. 
 
McKesson supports CMS’s proposed dual-standard approach and urges CMS to retain NCPDP 
standards for pharmacy benefit prior authorization workflows. A FHIR-only model will not support real-
world pharmacy prior authorization operations. NCPDP SCRIPT transactions already provide a mature 
request-response workflow for pharmacy benefit prior authorization in the provider and pharmacy 
setting, while medical benefit workflows still lack comparable, machine-interactable specificity regarding 
required data elements and clinical questions. CMS should therefore preserve NCPDP standards for 
provider and pharmacy workflows related to pharmacy benefit coverage and use this rule to push

Rich Buckley

medical benefit processes toward comparable clarity and responsiveness rather than force artificial 
standardization that degrades functionality. 
Section II.A.3. Required Standards for FHIR APIs 
McKesson supports the use of FHIR-based APIs where they improve consistency, transparency, and 
automation across impacted payer workflows. At the same time, CMS should ensure that required FHIR 
implementation does not override mature pharmacy standards or narrow participation to EHR-only 
environments. FHIR requirements should support interoperability across the broader care ecosystem, 
including pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, intermediary platforms, and workflow tools used by care 
teams in practice. 
Section II.A.4. Requiring Additional Implementation Guides to Support Interoperability APIs 
McKesson supports CMS’s efforts to strengthen implementation through additional technical guidance. 
CMS should ensure that implementation guide requirements are accompanied by clear documentation, 
realistic timelines, and operational expectations that reflect whether APIs are producing usable 
workflow integration rather than nominal compliance alone. 
Section II.A.5. Recommended Implementation Guides to Support Interoperability APIs and 
Request for Comment 
Where CMS recommends additional implementation guides or seeks comment on future standards 
adoption, McKesson encourages CMS to prioritize guides that improve real-world transaction 
specificity, machine-readable policy logic, and more actionable payer responses across both medical 
and pharmacy benefit workflows. 
 
Section II.B. Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Section II.B.3. Proposed Requirement to Incorporate Drugs Covered Under a Medical Benefit 
Into the Prior Authorization API for All Impacted Payers 
McKesson strongly supports expanding ePA requirements to drugs covered under a medical benefit 
and reducing reliance on manual processes such as fax-based submissions. We commend CMS for 
proposing to extend prior authorization API requirements to drugs and for recognizing the need to 
account for distinct operational realities across benefit types. 
CMS should also establish a clear expectation that prior authorization workflows for drugs transition 
fully out of fax-based processes and into electronic formats. While electronic prior authorization 
infrastructure is already widely available, inconsistent use and lack of payer requirements to process 
electronic submissions continue to drive administrative burden. We recommend that CMS require 
payers to accept and process prior authorization requests submitted electronically and support 
consistent adoption across providers, pharmacies, and care teams. 
 
Successful implementation will require CMS to address several operational issues directly. Benefit-
pathway ambiguity remains a significant source of delay, particularly for specialty and oncology 
therapies that may be billed under either the medical or pharmacy benefit depending on 
reimbursement, site-of-care, and patient affordability considerations. CMS should improve transparency 
around applicable pathways and response content without imposing rigid routing requirements that 
would undermine needed provider flexibility. For specialty drugs that may be covered under the medical 
McKesson Corporation 
6535 State Hwy 161 
Irving, TX 75039 
 
 
 
www.mckesson.com 
 
4 
 
Rich Buckley 
Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs 
 
benefit, Medicare Part D, or both, CMS should establish a standard 24-hour expedited timeframe for 
plans to provide timely coverage information, including whether the drug may be covered under one or 
both pathways and any applicable prior authorization requirements, so providers can pursue the option 
that best supports timely and appropriate patient care. To further reduce delays and administrative 
burden, we recommend that CMS require that, at the point of initial benefit eligibility inquiry, payers and 
PBMs provide machine-readable coverage criteria and prior authorization requirements for both 
medical and pharmacy benefits. These requirements should enable providers and care teams to 
populate prior authorization submissions efficiently without iterative back-and-forth. 
CMS should also require payers to oversee and align PBM-administered prior authorization criteria with 
payer medical policies to ensure consistency, reduce confusion, and avoid conflicting requirements 
across benefit pathways. 
Section II.B.7.b. Exceptions for Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated 
Exchanges 
To the extent CMS finalizes exceptions or phased implementation for Qualified Health Plan issuers on 
the Federally-facilitated Exchanges, McKesson encourages CMS to apply any flexibility in a manner 
that preserves the long-term goal of consistent, interoperable electronic prior authorization capabilities 
while recognizing operational readiness constraints. 
 
Section II.C. Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
Section II.C.2.c. Proposed Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial to Providers 
When Denying Prior Authorization of All Drugs for State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-Service 
Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Qualified Health 
Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
McKesson supports this objective and commends CMS for recognizing that clearer and more 
actionable denial communications are essential to reducing rework, improving provider understanding, 
and supporting more timely patient care. CMS should strengthen this provision while recognizing 
current standards limitations. Existing NCPDP SCRIPT transactions do not consistently support the full 
range of structured denial detail needed to make payer responses uniformly actionable, and denial 
rationale is often conveyed today through attachments or other unstructured fields. CMS should 
therefore require payers to provide complete, specific, and usable denial information during the 
transition period, while also advancing more standardized denial codes and response elements over 
time. Responses should identify what is missing, why a request was denied, and what clinical or 
utilization-management criteria apply—including any step-therapy requirements and applicable duration 
parameters—so providers and care teams can act without unnecessary rework. 
Section II.C.3.b. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Qualified Health Plan Issuers on 
the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
McKesson supports the goal of enhancing timeliness but notes that additional clarity is needed 
regarding how these timeframes will be operationalized. CMS should clarify that timing requirements 
must distinguish between an initial submission, a request for additional information, and a final 
determination. A nominal response immediately after receipt is not meaningful if it merely initiates 
repeated back-and-forth or shifts the request prematurely into denial and appeal. At a minimum, payers 
McKesson Corporation 
6535 State Hwy 161 
Irving, TX 75039 
 
 
 
www.mckesson.com 
 
5 
 
Rich Buckley 
Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs 
 
should be required to acknowledge receipt promptly, identify with specificity any missing information 
needed for review, and issue a substantive determination once a request is sufficiently complete to 
evaluate medical necessity. If a submission is incomplete, the payer should identify the missing 
elements with specificity and the determination clock should run from resubmission of the completed 
request rather than from an incomplete intake response alone. CMS should also establish a distinct 
front-end timeliness standard for specialty-drug coverage determinations. Where a specialty drug may 
be covered under the medical benefit, Medicare Part D, or both, plans should be required to provide a 
response within 24 hours that clarifies available coverage pathways and applicable prior authorization 
requirements before the substantive prior authorization timeframe begins. 
 
McKesson supports CMS’s effort to align timelines across programs, but those timelines must reflect 
how drug prior authorization functions in practice. Pharmacy benefit workflows already demonstrate 
that faster turnaround is possible when the required questions and response pathways are known up 
front. CMS should use that model to require more timely and more informative payer responses, 
particularly for medical benefit drug prior authorization, where lack of specificity remains a primary 
barrier to efficient review. 
Section II.C.3.c. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-
Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, and CHIP Managed Care Entities 
CMS should phase implementation and align timelines across related programs so that operational 
requirements, technical standards, and workflow expectations mature in a coordinated manner. That is 
especially important for Medicaid and other environments where operational readiness, vendor 
capacity, and benefit-administration complexity may vary significantly. Early technical guidance, staged 
adoption, and realistic transition periods will be necessary to avoid disruption and to ensure the final 
rule produces usable interoperability rather than nominal compliance. We recommend that CMS  further 
define phased implementation with a clear, time-bound glide path that prioritizes near-term elimination 
of fax-based workflows and progressive expansion of fully electronic prior authorization capabilities. For 
example, CMS could require near-term adoption of electronic submission and receipt standards, 
followed by subsequent phases that advance real-time processing, structured responses, and full 
workflow integration across all participants. 
 
CMS should ensure the final rule does not default to an EHR-centric implementation model. CMS 
should also explicitly recognize that prescribing is the initiation of an order within a broader workflow, 
and that prior authorization activities are frequently completed by office or health system staff, vendors 
with delegated authority, pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, or other care team members. Ensuring that 
these participants are able to initiate, submit, and manage electronic prior authorization transactions is 
essential to reducing administrative burden and improving efficiency. These teams frequently use 
intermediary tools and workflow applications that sit alongside the EHR. The rule should expressly 
preserve the ability of these participants to exchange information electronically, submit transactions 
where appropriate, and support timely care coordination across settings. CMS should also make clear 
that flexible user-permissioning and care-team access are necessary so these workflows can be 
completed by the personnel who actually perform them in practice. 
 
McKesson supports the long-term transition to standards-based electronic workflows, but CMS should 
distinguish between fragmented payer-specific portals and intermediary or EHR-connected tools that 
McKesson Corporation 
6535 State Hwy 161 
Irving, TX 75039 
 
 
 
www.mckesson.com 
 
6 
 
Rich Buckley 
Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs 
 
help providers and care teams complete transactions electronically. Many practices—particularly 
community, rural, and lower-resourced providers—still rely on web-based and hybrid tools because 
deep integration is not yet uniformly feasible. CMS should avoid eliminating these channels prematurely 
and instead focus on reducing reliance on disparate payer portals while preserving flexible electronic 
pathways that support care-team workflows. CMS should also require payer medical policies and 
related decision criteria to be available in accessible, machine-interactable formats rather than static 
documents that cannot be readily queried or operationalized, and those policies should be updated on 
a timely basis when new drugs or coverage requirements change. 
 
McKesson supports policies that promote appropriate data sharing while protecting patient privacy. 
CMS should reinforce minimum-necessary data expectations and make clear that payers should 
request only the information needed to assess coverage and medical necessity. Where additional 
information is required, payer responses should specify the exact missing elements rather than prompt 
wholesale submission of broad clinical records. This approach better protects patient privacy, reduces 
administrative burden, and aligns the rule with CMS’s broader goals for more targeted, interoperable, 
and usable data exchange. 
 
III. CONCLUSION 
McKesson supports CMS’s efforts to modernize prior authorization and interoperability for drugs and 
believes this proposed rule represents a meaningful step toward reducing administrative burden and 
improving patient access. 
To fully realize these benefits, CMS should ensure that implementation reflects real-world workflows 
across the healthcare ecosystem for both medical benefit and pharmacy benefit coverage, maintains 
flexibility through a dual-standard approach, and promotes transparency, accountability, and usability. 
Importantly, the rule should enable participation from all stakeholders—not just EHR-based actors—to 
support a truly interoperable system. 
We appreciate CMS’s leadership and look forward to continued engagement. If you have questions or 
need further information, please contact Fauzea Hussain, Vice President Public Policy  at 
Fauzea.Hussain@mckesson.com. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Rich Buckley 
 
Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** McKesson Corporation; signed by Rich Buckley, Senior Vice President, Corporate Affairs.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor / healthcare services organization / pharmacy and distribution stakeholder.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** McKesson describes an enterprise-wide role spanning community pharmacy, specialty care, oncology, distribution, health information technology, providers, pharmacies, payers, and technology developers.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

McKesson strongly supports extending interoperability and electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs, but urges CMS to reflect pharmacy, PBM, specialty pharmacy, provider, and intermediary workflows rather than an EHR-only model. It recommends preserving the dual FHIR/NCPDP standards framework, eliminating fax-based processes, requiring patient-specific machine-readable coverage criteria at initial eligibility inquiry, aligning payer and PBM requirements, strengthening actionable denial responses, and using phased implementation with clear glide paths.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; STATE/Medicaid implementation issues; GENERAL workflow and direct data entry concerns.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P. The comment refers to sections II.A, II.B, and II.C of the proposed rule but does not rely heavily on specific CFR citations.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR APIs; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP pharmacy ePA workflows; Prior Authorization API; patient-specific eligibility/coverage inquiry; structured denial codes; PBM/payer APIs; EHR-connected and intermediary tools.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Preserve dual-standard FHIR/NCPDP framework**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / clarify.
- **Rationale:** McKesson argues a FHIR-only approach would not support real-world pharmacy PA operations because NCPDP SCRIPT already provides mature request-response workflows for pharmacy benefit PA.
- **Specific request:** Retain NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit workflows and use FHIR where it improves medical benefit and payer API consistency.

**Topic 2: Transition fully away from fax-based PA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; EXISTING-WORKFLOWS
- **Position:** Modify / strengthen.
- **Rationale:** Fax-based submissions and inconsistent payer processing of electronic submissions drive administrative burden despite available ePA infrastructure.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to accept and process electronic PA requests and establish a clear glide path away from fax, including near-term electronic submission/receipt followed by real-time processing and structured responses.

**Topic 3: Machine-readable coverage criteria and benefit pathway clarity**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Modify / clarify.
- **Rationale:** Specialty and oncology therapies may be covered under medical, pharmacy, Medicare Part D, or multiple pathways depending on site of care, reimbursement, and affordability. Ambiguity causes delay and back-and-forth.
- **Specific request:** Require payers and PBMs to provide machine-readable coverage criteria and PA requirements at the point of initial benefit eligibility inquiry; require a 24-hour front-end response for specialty drugs to clarify available coverage pathways and PA requirements.

**Topic 4: PBM/payer alignment and broader care-team participation**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM; STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** PBM-administered requirements may conflict with payer medical policies; PA work is often performed by office staff, vendors, pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, and care-team members, not only ordering clinicians in EHRs.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to oversee and align PBM criteria with payer medical policies; explicitly preserve participation by pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, delegated vendors, intermediary tools, and non-physician care-team members with appropriate permissions.

**Topic 5: Actionable denial communications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with transition details.
- **Rationale:** Current NCPDP SCRIPT transactions may not consistently support all structured denial details; denials are often conveyed through unstructured attachments.
- **Specific request:** Require complete, specific, usable denial information during transition and advance standardized denial codes and response elements over time. Responses should identify missing information, denial basis, clinical/utilization-management criteria, step therapy requirements, and duration parameters.

**Topic 6: Timeframes and completeness rules**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Clarify / modify.
- **Rationale:** A nominal response is not meaningful if it only initiates repeated back-and-forth or premature denial. Timeframes must reflect initial submission, missing information requests, and final determination.
- **Specific request:** Require prompt acknowledgement, specificity on missing information, and a substantive determination once a request is complete; clarify when the clock starts; use pharmacy workflow lessons to push medical benefit PA toward faster, informative responses.

**Topic 7: Phased implementation and QHP flexibility**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; STATE-EXTENSION-PROCESS
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Operational readiness, Medicaid/PBM/vendor complexity, and marketplace constraints may vary.
- **Specific request:** Adopt clear phased implementation with time-bound expectations, preserve long-term consistent electronic capabilities, and avoid an EHR-centric model.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1-S3, S18, S32, S37 (FHIR IGs):** Supports FHIR APIs where useful, but warns against overriding mature pharmacy standards and asks for real-world workflow integration and machine-readable policy logic.
- **S12, S15, S21, S28 (medical benefit drugs):** Strong response; supports inclusion of medical benefit drugs and asks for benefit-pathway transparency and front-end coverage determination.
- **S14, S19, S22, S25, S31 (pharmacy benefit drugs):** Strong response; preserve NCPDP SCRIPT and pharmacy ePA infrastructure; avoid FHIR-only design.
- **S16-S17 (denial reasons):** Strong response; require complete, usable, structured denial information and advance standardized denial codes.
- **S20, S43 (timeframes):** Requests clarity on clock-start rules, missing information, and front-end specialty-drug pathway responses within 24 hours.
- **S40-S42 (QHP exceptions):** Supports limited phased flexibility if consistent with long-term electronic PA capability.
- **S44-S56 (HIPAA standards):** Addresses interaction of FHIR and NCPDP standards, urging preservation of dual standards and practical workflows.
- **S66-S82 / direct data entry and workflow RFI:** Addresses need to move away from fragmented fax/payer portals while preserving intermediary and EHR-connected tools that support actual care-team workflows.
- **Other solicitations:** Endpoint publication, Open Payments CMP, and ONC standards are less central than workflow and standards-choice issues.

## 6. THEMES

- TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY
- EXISTING-WORKFLOWS
- VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM
- MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- STANDARDS-MATURITY
- PROVIDER-BURDEN
- PATIENT-ACCESS
- IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE
- STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION
- TRANSPARENCY

## 7. POTENTIAL CMS ACTION ITEMS

1. Preserve NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit PA while requiring FHIR where appropriate.
2. Require payers to accept and process electronic PA submissions and phase out fax reliance.
3. Require patient-specific, machine-readable coverage criteria and PA requirements at initial eligibility/benefit inquiry.
4. Clarify coverage pathway response obligations for specialty drugs, including 24-hour front-end pathway responses.
5. Require payer oversight and alignment of PBM PA criteria with payer medical policy.
6. Ensure APIs and authorization workflows can be used by pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, delegated vendors, and care-team staff.
7. Define denial response elements and build toward standardized structured denial codes.
8. Adopt phased implementation with clear milestones.

## 8. NOTABLE QUOTES / EVIDENCE

- McKesson states that a FHIR-only model will not support real-world pharmacy prior authorization operations.
- The comment stresses that implementation should not default to an EHR-centric model because PA work is often performed by office staff, pharmacies, specialty pharmacies, or delegated vendors.
- McKesson recommends machine-readable coverage criteria at initial benefit eligibility inquiry to reduce iterative back-and-forth.

## 9. OVERALL ASSESSMENT

McKesson provides a technically detailed support-with-modifications comment from a pharmacy/technology ecosystem perspective. Its highest-priority asks are dual-standard preservation, machine-readable coverage criteria, PBM alignment, care-team workflow access, phased implementation, and actionable denial responses.
